displayQuote: If you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail

meta.title: Who really said "If you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: John Wooden didn't coin it. The line appeared verbatim in The Biblical World in January 1919 — quoting Rev. H. K. Williams — when Wooden was eight years old.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail'?
meta.ogDescription: Not John Wooden, and not Ben Franklin. The exact sentence is in print in The Biblical World, January 1919, credited to Rev. H. K. Williams.

answer.label: Not John Wooden — an old proverb, in print by 1919
answer.authorDates: fl. 1919 · Clergyman, writing in Young People’s Service
answer.sourceLine: The wording is genuine and very old — it simply isn’t Wooden’s. The exact sentence closes a short item of advice reprinted in The Biblical World, January 1919 ↗: “Remember, if you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail,” credited there to Rev. H. K. Williams. Quote Investigator ↗ calls this the first match it has found, treats the saying as proverbial wisdom of anonymous origin, and expects earlier instances to turn up — so Williams is best described as the earliest documented voice, not the coiner.

source.heading: The 1919 printing

docMeta.dd: The Biblical World, Vol. 53, No. 1 (University of Chicago Press), January 1919, pp. 80–81
Rev. H. K. Williams, writing “in the Young People’s Service”
John Wooden (1910–2010), whose earliest documented use is a January 1977 speech

source.excerpt: Take full advantage of all the lesson helps that are at your disposal. Do some serious thinking yourself. Be well prepared and brief in your remarks. There is positively no excuse for wasting another’s time by going to the meeting unprepared and rambling helplessly in your talk. Remember, if you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail.
trail: January 1919 — the exact wording, in print. “Remember, if you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail” appears verbatim in the scanned text of The Biblical World, Vol. 53, No. 1 ↗, credited to Rev. H. K. Williams. John Wooden was eight years old.

1929 and 1970 — the saying spreads, then acquires a famous name. Quote Investigator ↗ records South Carolina schools superintendent James H. Hope using “If we fail to prepare we prepare to fail” without attribution in a 1929 annual report, and a 1970 filler item in The Minneapolis Tribune printing “By failing to prepare you are preparing to fail” over the name of Benjamin Franklin.

21 January 1977 — Wooden’s first documented use. Per Quote Investigator ↗, the Lubbock Avalanche-Journal reported Wooden telling an audience at Texas Tech’s University Center Theatre: “When you fail to prepare, you’re preparing to fail” — a variant, and decades downstream of the printed record.

Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed.” The John Wooden page ↗ lists “Failing to prepare is preparing to fail” in its Misattributed section, noting that Wooden “only repeated a common aphorism” already circulating when he was a youth.
source.excerptNote: The line is the closing flourish of practical advice to young people running church meetings — not a sports maxim. The Biblical World ran the item under its “The Church and the World” department, introducing it as “Rev. H. K. Williams, in the Young People’s Service, writes as follows.” Transcribed from the scanned issue at the Internet Archive.

source.rightsNote: The work containing the earliest documented instance — The Biblical World, Vol. 53, No. 1, published by the University of Chicago Press in January 1919 — was first published well before 1931, so the issue and this passage are in the public domain in the United States. The 1919 date is confirmed on the scanned issue itself ↗, not inferred.

author.name: Rev. H. K. Williams
author.heading: The minister behind the first printing
author.metaLine: fl. 1919 · Clergyman, writing in Young People’s Service
author.bio: Almost nothing is documented about him. He surfaces in the record as “Rev. H. K. Williams,” a contributor to the periodical Young People’s Service, whose short article on organising church youth societies — “The Group Plan” — was reprinted by The Biblical World in January 1919. Its final sentence is the earliest appearance of this saying that anyone has yet located. He is not known to have coined it: Quote Investigator suspects he was passing along an adage already in circulation, and no biography, dates or further writings have been tied to him in the course of this check.

copyAttribution: "Remember, if you fail to prepare, you are preparing to fail." — Rev. H. K. Williams, quoted in "The Group Plan," The Biblical World 53, no. 1 (January 1919): 81. Commonly credited to John Wooden or Benjamin Franklin; Wikiquote lists it as misattributed to both, and Quote Investigator traces the earliest known printing to Williams in 1919 while treating the saying itself as an anonymous proverb.

misattribution.heading: Two famous names, neither of them right
misattribution.intro: This is a sentence with no shortage of borrowed fathers. Both of the big ones are documented misattributions — and one of them is repeated by the people who manage John Wooden’s own legacy.

items.why: Wikiquote’s John Wooden page ↗ places “Failing to prepare is preparing to fail” in its Misattributed section, stating that Wooden “only repeated a common aphorism” that “was already in circulation as early as the 1920s, when he was a youth.” He did use it — Quote Investigator ↗ documents a variant in a 21 January 1977 speech — but the printed record runs back to 1919.

Wikiquote’s Benjamin Franklin page ↗ lists “By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail” under Misattributed, noting flatly that “there is no evidence that he coined any forms of this quote.” Quote Investigator ↗ traces the Franklin tag to a 1970 filler item in The Minneapolis Tribune — 180 years after Franklin died.

The official Wooden site tags the line both ways: one article at thewoodeneffect.com ↗ presents “Failure to prepare is preparing to fail” as one of Wooden’s favourite maxims, while another page on the same site credits the Franklin form. Notably, even the estate frames it as a saying Wooden favoured — not one he wrote.

misattribution.truthLine: No one has established who coined it. Quote Investigator ↗ classes the saying as proverbial wisdom with an anonymous origin, and suspects Rev. H. K. Williams was himself repeating an adage already in circulation — so the honest answer is: an anonymous proverb, first found in print in 1919, later adopted by a famous coach.

context.heading: A church-meeting tip, not a locker-room maxim
lead: The sentence people now hear in Nike-adjacent tones was written for teenagers who had to run a Wednesday-evening young people’s meeting. Williams’s piece, “The Group Plan,” is administrative housekeeping: split your society into four groups, give each one meeting a month, make the leader convene his group a fortnight ahead so every member gets a part. The famous line is the last sentence — a warning against turning up and “rambling helplessly in your talk.”

That domestic origin is exactly why the saying travelled so well. It carries no field, no jargon and no author, which makes it easy to re-home — onto a founding father in 1970, onto a basketball coach after 1977. The wording survived intact for more than a century; only the name attached to it kept changing.
detailsBody: The documented chain, per Quote Investigator. 1919: Rev. H. K. Williams, The Biblical World — “if you fail to prepare you are preparing to fail.” 1929: James H. Hope, South Carolina superintendent of education — “If we fail to prepare we prepare to fail,” unattributed. 1941: Quartermaster General E. B. Gregory — “For us to fail to prepare, is to prepare to fail.” 1970: The Minneapolis Tribune pins it on Franklin. 1977: Wooden uses a variant in Lubbock, Texas.

Why we do not call Williams the author. Quote Investigator says only that his is the first match it has found, hypothesises that he was drawing on an adage already circulating, and expects future researchers to find earlier instances. We have confirmed his 1919 text against the scan; we have not confirmed — and no one has — that he invented it.
